This tool aims to counteract technology-enabled cognitive security risks, where abusers use the internet and mobile technology to manipulate and control their victims. Rather than a simple chatbot, the AI will function as a personalized coach that learns from an abuser's tactics and the survivor's responses. It will then alert the user to potential online abuse and cognitive manipulation, offering suggestions based on the survivor's specific recovery goals and risk factors. This initiative combines cybersecurity, AI, and psychology to address the often-overlooked area of digital security in the context of intimate partner violence. <3> The city of Philadelphia's annual 'Paint Philly Purple' campaign took place to show support for domestic violence survivors and raise awareness as part of Domestic Violence Awareness Month. [2, 5] The event in 2023 occurred on Thursday, October 19, 2023. [2, 5] This timing aligns with the national 'Purple Thursday,' a day of action held on the third Thursday of October. [10] To participate, the city encouraged residents to wear purple, take a selfie, and post it on social media with the hashtag #PaintPhillyPurple to start conversations about domestic violence. [2] The date of the event changes annually; in 2022 it was on October 20, and in 2024 it was scheduled for October 17. [3, 4, 6] <4> On September 8, 2023, the Supreme Court of Erie County, New York, issued a decision granting a re-sentencing hearing for a domestic violence survivor under the state's Domestic Violence Survivors Justice Act (DVSJA). [19] The defendant, who had pleaded guilty to Manslaughter in the First Degree on May 23, 2017, successfully moved for the hearing, which was conducted on June 22, 2023. [19] The court determined that the defendant was a victim of substantial abuse, which was a significant factor in the crime's commission. [19] This ruling exemplifies the application of the DVSJA, a law that allows courts to impose less severe, alternative sentences on defendants who have been victims of domestic violence. The court ordered that the defendant be resentenced in accordance with the provisions of Penal Law §60.12. [19] <5> On July 28, 2023, President Joe Biden signed an executive order fundamentally reforming the U.S. military justice system's approach to serious crimes, including sexual assault, domestic violence, child abuse, and murder. [1, 2, 5] This order shifted the critical authority to decide whether to prosecute these offenses from military commanders to newly established Offices of Special Trial Counsel (OSTC), which are comprised of independent, specialized military prosecutors. [1, 2, 6] The action, which amends the Manual for Courts-Martial, represents the most significant overhaul of the Uniform Code of Military Justice (UCMJ) since its establishment in 1950. [2, 4] This reform was a key recommendation from the Independent Review Commission on Sexual Assault in the Military and formally implements bipartisan legislation passed by Congress in 2022 after years of advocacy by lawmakers like Senator Kirsten Gillibrand. They urged States, UN agencies, and other key actors to commit to ending violence against older persons by strengthening data collection systems to properly address the problem. [1, 7] The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce. [6, 8, 9] Original cosponsors of the bill include Representatives Brian K. Fitzpatrick, Gwen Moore, and Young Kim. [7] The legislation aims to improve and expand services for domestic violence survivors by reauthorizing the Family Violence and Prevention Services program through FY2028 and increasing the funding authorization level to address low per-program funding. [1] It also seeks to broaden support for prevention services and enhance services for underserved communities, including culturally specific programs for racial and ethnic minority groups and dedicated resources for tribal coalitions and a hotline for Native Americans affected by domestic violence. metadata.original_text: This time series records domestic violence data in the web search domain, with a collection frequency of weekly, focusing on monitoring and analyzing relevant indicators. Prediction target period: from 2024-02-18 to 2024-05-05. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> February is officially recognized as Teen Dating Violence Awareness Month in the United States, an initiative established by Congress in 2010. The month is dedicated to educating teenagers and young adults about the characteristics of healthy relationships and the warning signs of abuse. As highlighted by proclamations from entities like the Michigan Governor's Office, the observance aims to empower young people and encourage dialogue between adults and teens about building respectful connections. <2> The U.S. Department of Justice's Office on Violence Against Women (OVW) finalized its grant awards for Fiscal Year 2023, which concluded on September 30, 2023. While a single, comprehensive announcement date is not available, a grant recipient reported the award on December 13, 2023, stating that the OVW awarded 828 grants totaling $633,444,382. [3] An earlier, more specific announcement on October 11, 2023, detailed $68,196,816 in grants to American Indian and Alaska Native communities. [4] The funding supports a wide array of programs designed to combat domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, and stalking. [3, 4] This includes grants to enhance culturally specific services for victims and programs that engage men and boys as allies in preventing violence. [2, 5] The official lists of all grant recipients for FY 2023 are published on the Department of Justice website, organized by state and program. [1, 2] <3> The Illinois Department of Human Services (IDHS) announced a Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) for up to $9 million in competitive grants for organizations that provide health and behavioral health services to survivors of domestic violence and their dependents. [1, 2] This initiative, funded by the American Rescue Plan Act through the Family Violence Prevention Services Act, aimed to enhance the safety, sustainability, and capacity of the domestic violence advocacy workforce. [1, 2] The primary goal of the awards is to expand access to these crucial services for survivors. [1, 2] The application period for this funding opportunity concluded on December 10, 2023. [1, 2] <4> On October 31, 2023, the U.S. Department of Justice's Office on Violence Against Women (OVW) published a blog post titled "DVAM 2023: Ending Domestic Violence Requires Us All to Work Together" to mark Domestic Violence Awareness and Prevention Month. [1] The post reflects on the collective progress made in addressing domestic violence and underscores that a collaborative, coordinated community response is essential to ending it. [2] It emphasizes that survivors are at the core of the OVW's mission and highlights the importance of providing survivor-centered services and fostering strong partnerships with community organizations to ensure the safety of survivors and their children. [1, 3] <5> On September 29, 2023, President Joe Biden issued a proclamation designating October 2023 as National Domestic Violence Awareness and Prevention Month. The proclamation underscored the administration's thirty-year commitment to ending gender-based violence, referencing the original Violence Against Women Act (VAWA) of 1990. It highlighted significant legislative achievements and financial commitments, including bringing the federal investment for gender-based violence programs to $700 million in 2023—the highest in history—and proposing $1 billion for the following year's budget. The announcement also mentioned the first-ever National Plan to End Gender-Based Violence as a comprehensive strategy to address the issue. <6> Researchers at the Georgia Institute of Technology announced on September 26, 2023, that they are developing a new software tool powered by artificial intelligence to support domestic abuse survivors. This tool aims to counteract technology-enabled cognitive security risks, where abusers use the internet and mobile technology to manipulate and control their victims. Rather than a simple chatbot, the AI will function as a personalized coach that learns from an abuser's tactics and the survivor's responses. It will then alert the user to potential online abuse and cognitive manipulation, offering suggestions based on the survivor's specific recovery goals and risk factors. This initiative combines cybersecurity, AI, and psychology to address the often-overlooked area of digital security in the context of intimate partner violence. <7> The city of Philadelphia's annual 'Paint Philly Purple' campaign took place to show support for domestic violence survivors and raise awareness as part of Domestic Violence Awareness Month. [2, 5] The event in 2023 occurred on Thursday, October 19, 2023. [2, 5] This timing aligns with the national 'Purple Thursday,' a day of action held on the third Thursday of October. [10] To participate, the city encouraged residents to wear purple, take a selfie, and post it on social media with the hashtag #PaintPhillyPurple to start conversations about domestic violence. [2] The date of the event changes annually; in 2022 it was on October 20, and in 2024 it was scheduled for October 17. [3, 4, 6] <8> On September 8, 2023, the Supreme Court of Erie County, New York, issued a decision granting a re-sentencing hearing for a domestic violence survivor under the state's Domestic Violence Survivors Justice Act (DVSJA). [19] The defendant, who had pleaded guilty to Manslaughter in the First Degree on May 23, 2017, successfully moved for the hearing, which was conducted on June 22, 2023. [19] The court determined that the defendant was a victim of substantial abuse, which was a significant factor in the crime's commission. [19] This ruling exemplifies the application of the DVSJA, a law that allows courts to impose less severe, alternative sentences on defendants who have been victims of domestic violence. The court ordered that the defendant be resentenced in accordance with the provisions of Penal Law §60.12. [19] <9> On July 28, 2023, President Joe Biden signed an executive order fundamentally reforming the U.S. military justice system's approach to serious crimes, including sexual assault, domestic violence, child abuse, and murder. [1, 2, 5] This order shifted the critical authority to decide whether to prosecute these offenses from military commanders to newly established Offices of Special Trial Counsel (OSTC), which are comprised of independent, specialized military prosecutors. [1, 2, 6] The action, which amends the Manual for Courts-Martial, represents the most significant overhaul of the Uniform Code of Military Justice (UCMJ) since its establishment in 1950. [2, 4] This reform was a key recommendation from the Independent Review Commission on Sexual Assault in the Military and formally implements bipartisan legislation passed by Congress in 2022 after years of advocacy by lawmakers like Senator Kirsten Gillibrand. [1, 2, 3]

Events such as Wear Blue Day, scheduled for April 4, 2025, and various local and national activities are organized throughout the month to raise awareness and inspire action. The murder occurred on January 27, 2025. While her father confessed to his involvement in the premeditated crime, police reports indicate that her maternal uncle, Muhammad Tayyab, was the one who shot her. [3, 5] A public reception for the artists was held on April 3, 2025. In contrast, the study found that the associations for men were not statistically significant.

metadata.original_text: This time series records domestic violence data in the web search domain, with a collection frequency of weekly, focusing on monitoring and analyzing relevant indicators. Prediction target period: from 2025-11-23 to 2026-02-08. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> A bill titled the 'Better Care For Domestic Violence Survivors Act' (H.R.5702) was introduced in the U.S. House of Representatives on October 6, 2025, by Representative Emilia Strong Sykes. The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary on the same day. The legislation aims to amend the Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act of 1994 by establishing a demonstration program to provide trauma-informed, victim-centered training for healthcare providers to better assist survivors of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, and stalking. The bill proposes authorizing appropriations of $10 million for each fiscal year from 2026 through 2030 to carry out the program. <2> On October 2, 2025, San Diego County District Attorney Summer Stephan, along with the San Diego Domestic Violence Council, community leaders, and survivors, launched Domestic Violence Awareness Month with a ceremony in Chula Vista. The event's theme was 'Hope and Healing, Families for Change' and it was the first of five such events planned throughout the county for October. The gathering served to raise awareness, remember those who lost their lives to domestic violence in the past year, and share resources with the community. Highlights included a resource fair and a candlelight vigil to honor victims. During the event, it was announced that the new 'One Safe Place: The South County Family Justice Center' would be opening later that month in National City to provide survivors with comprehensive, co-located support services. The center officially opened with a ribbon-cutting ceremony on October 17, 2025, offering a range of no-cost services for survivors of domestic violence, child abuse, sexual assault, and other crimes. <3> On October 1, 2025, marking the beginning of Domestic Violence Awareness Month, the National Network to End Domestic Violence (NNEDV) issued an urgent warning regarding a potential government shutdown. The organization cautioned that a shutdown threatens to delay federal funding and lead to program closures, which would have devastating consequences for domestic violence survivors and their children who depend on these essential services. <4> The City of Philadelphia's Office of Domestic Violence Strategies and its community partners will hold several events for Domestic Violence Awareness Month in October 2025. Activities will commence on Wednesday, October 1, 2025, with two key events. The '2nd Annual DV Awareness Walk, Jog, & Run' will take place on the Benjamin Franklin Bridge from 9:30 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. Following this, Women Against Abuse will host the 18th Annual iPledge® Campaign press conference and resource fair from 12:00 p.m. to 1:00 p.m. in the Philadelphia City Hall Courtyard. The press conference, part of a campaign with the theme of HOPE, will feature speakers and honor State Representative Joanna E. McClinton for her advocacy. These events aim to unite community members, elected officials, survivors, and advocates to raise awareness and support for those affected by domestic violence. <5> The Mary Kay Ash Foundation and The National Domestic Violence Hotline have renewed their partnership to launch a nationwide educational campaign, announced on August 12, 2025. The initiative, which commenced around August 1, 2025, is focused on providing trauma-informed education, community engagement resources, and life-saving tools to help the public recognize and respond to domestic abuse. The campaign includes offerings such as live virtual training sessions and downloadable toolkits with conversation guides. <6> On August 7, 2025, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of New Mexico announced that Miranda Cachini, a 26-year-old enrolled member of the Zuni Pueblo, was indicted on federal charges for child abuse resulting in death. The indictment alleges that on January 26, 2025, Cachini allowed a minor child to be placed in a dangerous situation which ultimately led to the child's death. Cachini faces charges of abuse of a child resulting in death. <7> The Office for Victims of Crime (OVC), part of the Department of Justice, announced the "FY 2025 Emergency and Transitional Pet Shelter and Housing Assistance for Victims of Domestic Violence Program." This notice of funding opportunity aims to provide funding for shelter, transitional housing, and other assistance to support victims of domestic violence and their companion animals, which include pets, service animals, emotional support animals, and horses. The grant program recognizes that a majority of domestic violence shelters do not accommodate pets, forcing victims to choose between their safety and leaving a beloved animal behind. The initiative seeks to increase the number of shelter beds and housing options that can accommodate both survivors and their animals, thereby removing a significant barrier to safety. <8> A mid-year 2025 report from the Council on Criminal Justice (CCJ) on crime trends in U.S. cities found that domestic violence was the only offense out of 13 studied to increase in the first half of 2025 compared to the same period in 2024. [1, 2, 4] The report, which analyzed data from 42 cities, showed an overall increase of 3% in reported domestic violence incidents. [1] The most significant monthly increases compared to the previous year were observed in February (+15%) and March (+6%) 2025. [1] While 11 other offenses, including homicide and robbery, decreased, drug offenses remained at the same level as the prior year. [1, 2] <9> The 'Tech Safety for Victims of Domestic Violence, Dating Violence, Sexual Assault, and Stalking Act' (S.2159) was introduced in the U.S. Senate on June 25, 2025. On the same day, the bill was read twice and then referred to the Committee on the Judiciary for further consideration. The bipartisan legislation was reintroduced by Representatives Debbie Dingell and Zach Nunn, along with Senator Ron Wyden, to help prevent abusers from using technology to stalk, harass, or control survivors. <10> The 'Tech Safety for Victims of Domestic Violence, Dating Violence, Sexual Assault, and Stalking Act' (H.R.4127, S.2159) was introduced in the U.S. House of Representatives and the Senate by a bipartisan group including Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR) and Reps. Debbie Dingell (D-MI) and Zach Nunn (R-IA). The legislation aims to combat technology-enabled abuse, such as online harassment and stalking, by establishing a five-year pilot program. This program would provide up to 15 grants of $2 million each to clinics and partnerships to support survivors, which includes services like purchasing new, secure devices. Additionally, the bill proposes a separate grant program of up to $20 million for non-profits and higher education institutions to develop training and provide technical assistance for groups working to prevent tech-enabled abuse.
